content.thinking:
I'm planning the design: a whimsical capybara with a bird perched on its head, going for a storybook feel with a barrel-shaped body and blunt head based on realistic proportions, keeping the scene rich but manageable to build in one pass.

I'm working out the skeleton structure carefully, placing the hips joint and planning the spine chain from tail to head, thinking through how root joints and parented chains interact in the API so I avoid duplicate joints or structural errors.

Adding neck chain with two joints and a head joint attached at the end, keeping the neck short since capybaras have stubby necks. For the body itself I'm planning a sweep along a catmull path running from the rump through hips, spine, and neck, defining the bone list and starting to set up a radius function for the silhouette shape.

Defining body profile curve...

For the coat, I'm thinking russet-brown with a lighter countershaded belly, using a mottled texture for subtle fur variation and a cel-shaded lighting pass for the whimsical look.

Now I'm working out the leg rig—four short legs using a simple limb chain for front legs and a bent-hock structure for the hind legs, calculating joint positions and reach distances so the proportions stay anatomically plausible for a capybara.

Checking the distances confirm a reasonably bent chain for the 3-segment hind leg, with 2 inner joints needing 2 bend hints. For naming, since there are 3 spans I need 4 joint names including the tip, so I'll go with hipL, kneeL, hockL, footL per side, tagged with role "leg".

The hip should connect to the parent hips bone, rooted inside the body surface where it's safely buried under the torso capsule. For leg thickness I'm tapering the radii from 0.07 down to 0.05 along the chain. For feet, I need toes — capybaras have 4 front toes and 3 hind toes with partial webbing and small hoof-like nails, so I'm planning to fan out small capsules from each foot tip to represent digits, plus tiny dark nail spikes at the ends.

I'll keep the toes as rigid geometry riding on the foot bone rather than adding separate joints, to limit rigging complexity. For foot placement, I'm positioning the sole near ground level with a flattened dark paw pad ellipsoid, and adding forward-pointing toe capsules just above it.

Now I'm moving on to the head: a blunt capybara-style snout with high nostrils, small side-set eyes, rounded ears at the back, and a split upper lip, built from lofted or combined ellipsoid shapes anchored at a forward-angled neck joint.

Checking proportions with round caps at the ends — the head ends up bigger than the shoulders, which is fine for a whimsical exaggerated look even though real capybaras have lower heads relative to their withers. I'm nudging the head center down slightly and placing the bird joint on top of the head where it'll perch.

Working out the jaw and skull geometry...

Realizing the round cap dome actually extends beyond the path end by its radius, so I need to pull the snout path back earlier to keep the true front edge where I want it—otherwise the head would reach too far forward. I'm reconsidering a blunter, flatter snout shape to match a capybara's actual face instead of a tapered rounded cap.

Since I can't actually measure anything, I need to estimate everything carefully and commit to values. I'm sketching out head station coordinates (position, width, height) across four cross-sections tapering from the base near z0.38 up to a rounded cap around z0.85, keeping the head extending roughly 0.35 units beyond the body.

I'll trim the final station a bit and slightly exaggerate the head size for a whimsical look, then place the nose pad as a small dark ellipsoid protruding from the snout front, with two tiny nostril pads positioned near the top of the snout.

Calculating the dome's curvature to find the correct y-position for the nostrils, factoring in the radius falloff at that distance along the profile — settling on placing small dark spheres there, partially embedded in the surface, which should look fine. I'm considering switching to a surface-query approach for more robust placement going forward.

For eyes, I'm thinking of a simple sphere construction: a black bead with a white highlight sphere offset slightly. I'm interpolating the head's half-width between two reference points to figure out where on the z-axis the eyes should sit, aiming for a position that's high and mid-head like a real capybara.

I'll skip eyelashes and brow tuft and just add a thin brown sweep above the eye for a subtle lid line. Now I'm placing the ears as small rounded shapes near the top back of the head, using flattened ellipsoids for the brown outer and a pink inner ellipsoid for the detail, positioning them symmetrically on both sides.

Calculating the rotation...

For the inner ear, I'll add a smaller pink ellipsoid offset toward the front. Now I'm adding whimsical details like cheek blush as small flattened discs near the eyes, and thin whisker rods extending outward from the muzzle sides.

I'm also skipping a detailed lip cleft and instead adding a simple dark lip line, plus a lower jaw shape and two cute little buck teeth peeking over the lower lip for a whimsical touch, positioned just under the nose in a pale yellow tone.

For the jaw itself, I'm building a tapered frustum box oriented upward from the head's underside toward the front, giving it a wider back and narrower front, then planning a rounded chin sphere at the front tip to soften the shape.

Checking the overlap between head bottom and jaw top — it nestles fine, slightly overlapping which works for a jaw rigged to the head bone, colored a lighter tan "#d9b27c" with a joint at the chin pointing forward, parented to head. Now I'm thinking about the small bird perched on the head — a whimsical little songbird, maybe bluish with an orange breast for a cute pop of color.

Now I'm figuring out the bird's full skeleton: body, head, tail, wings, upper/lower beak, legs, all parented to the head joint. Positioning it on top of the skull between the ears and forehead, with a chubby sunken body around 12cm, and deciding whether it should face forward or sideways.

I'll have the bird face forward like a little sentry, add tiny orange legs with toes gripping into the fur from belly to scalp, and consider small whimsical touches like a tiny flower tucked near the ear for extra charm.

Now for fur texture, I'll scatter around 500 small card-based tufts across the body using a lean and backward flow, each with low triangle cost so it stays cheap—about 2000 triangles total. The tuft texture itself I'll draw as a grey-white tapered SVG shape so it can be tinted by the coat's paint color at the root, keeping it consistent with the cel-shaded lighting.

For the head I'll skip cards except small cheek tufts, using a tighter scatter. With lean around 70°, the cards lie nearly flat against the surface rather than standing edge-on, so from above they read as short fur strips rather than slivers—that's the look I want, so I'll disable cross-facing. Hair hits will just inherit bone weights from the surface, and next I'm thinking about toon cel shading for a whimsical stylized finish.

Since capybaras have only a vestigial tail, I'll skip a full tail but add a tiny nub joint on the rump with a small brown sphere for silhouette completeness, keeping the rig simple. Now I'm laying out the body joint hierarchy starting from hips as root and building the spine chain upward.

Continuing with spine joints...

Head joint sits near z=0.46, parented to neck2, with its bone aiming forward and slightly down. The body sweep should taper to a smaller radius right before it meets the head so the head geometry can take over cleanly, so I need to check the end radius against the head's width to avoid awkward overlap.

I'm shrinking the body's end radius to 0.125 to avoid coinciding exactly with the head's surface. Checking the head's vertical extent against the body's top profile confirms things line up reasonably, and now I'm mapping out the spine of the body sweep path from rump to shoulders with coordinates shifting upward and forward along the way.

Working through the radius keys along that path, I realize the rump cap pushes the total length to about 1.42m, longer than typical, so I pull the start point forward slightly to compress it to roughly 1.3m while keeping the chubby, rounded look.

Checking the barrel width (~0.45m) against where legs attach, I confirm the leg roots at x=±0.15 with their 0.055 radius stay flush with the body surface at hip height rather than poking out awkwardly.

Now I'm setting up the front leg chain with two bone segments and a bend direction pointing backward, naming the joints shoulder, elbow, and wrist, and parenting them to the spine joint near the shoulder region around z=0.25.

For taper I'll use a radius function that shrinks linearly along the chain from 0.065 to 0.045. The limb function returns a polyline that gets skinned smoothly even at the knee bend, with one joint per span. I'm placing the front legs at x=±0.15, z=0.22, and the rear legs at x=±0.15, z=-0.33, parented to the hips.

For the hind legs I'm scaling up the thigh since capybaras have thick haunches, sweeping radius from 0.09 down to 0.045 across a three-segment chain with lengths 0.17, 0.15, and 0.09. The final segment runs vertically like a cannon bone so the foot lands flat, and I'm adding toe capsules extending forward from the foot base to give it some visual detail.

Adding toe nails and paw pads...

For the foot bones I'll use the tip joint from the chain if it exists, checking that both the 3-name and 4-name joint cases resolve correctly to the last joint. Now I'm settling on a whimsical warm russet-ginger coat with a cream belly and a darker muzzle and back streak for visual contrast.

Building fur texture palette...

Adding leg gradients and head paint next, darkening the lower legs and blending the muzzle color into the head using a gradient over the countershaded fur. I'm keeping the chin a flat cream tone and planning a small sphere for the tail nub before moving on to designing the bluebird — a round, whimsical body starting with a basic sphere.

Now I'm planning out the bird's anatomy and joint hierarchy: separate head sphere, cone beak, tucked wing ellipsoids, spiky tail feathers, orange breast, crest tufts, and leg joints, all parented under the body through named roles like jaw, wing, tail, and leg. I'm starting to set the actual coordinates and radii for the body sphere's position in the model.

Adding tiny gripping toes, then a chubby bluebird head merged into the body with a layered orange beak spike for upper and lower mandible.

Now I'm positioning the eye beads just outside the head sphere's surface, checking distances from center to make sure they sit right at the facet edge with small white highlight dots.

For the crest, I'm placing three small spikes near the top of the head tilted backward in deep blue. For the wings, I'm shaping flattened ellipsoids on each side of the body, tilting them slightly downward and outward to suggest a folded, fanned position.

Now I'm adding flight feathers at the wing rear using thin extruded feather shapes rather than simple cones, defining a tapered leaf-like outline for a more natural feather look.

I'm working out the orientation math so the feather's thickness axis aligns correctly along the wing surface, computing the cross product of direction vectors to confirm the thickness runs along the right axis, then varying the fan direction per feather index to spread them out.

Computing cross products for wing thickness, then setting up tail feathers behind the body with perpendicular axes so they fan out sideways while staying flat.

Maybe I'll add a small daisy accessory on the capybara's ear—a yellow sphere center with six petals arranged in a ring, using flattened sphere parts oriented outward along each ring item's facing axis.

I'm positioning the daisy near the left ear base, facing outward and slightly up and forward, with 8 white petals around a small yellow center sphere, sized to look cute at roughly 0.07 diameter overall. I'm figuring out which bone to attach the flower's frame to, likely the head since there's no dedicated ear joint.

I'm also recalculating the head's surface geometry to check if the flower's placement is actually sitting on the skin or floating above it—working through the ellipse math at that height and depth to adjust the y-coordinate downward so it sits correctly, and doing the same check for the ear positions.

I'm checking if that position collides with the wing, so I'm trying alternate placements—near the right ear, tucked behind it, or near the neck—computing head-surface coordinates each time to avoid overlapping other features before settling on tucking the daisy near the ear front.

Checking the daisy placement against the wing boundary confirms it fits, with the flower centered near [0.105, 0.612, 0.47] and offset slightly along its direction vector onto the dome surface. Now I'm verifying the capybara's eye positions at x=±0.132, z=0.58, y=0.54, cross-referencing against the head width constraints from the surface spheres at that z-depth.

Computing the eye bead geometry — radius 0.03, protruding about 0.027 from the surface with a small white highlight sphere offset toward the upper-outer corner. I'm considering whether to add a subtle brow sweep or lash detail for whimsy, sketching a thin curved rod along the upper eye socket.

Checking brow placement: at x=.13 the dome surface sits at y≈.574, just below the eye, so the brow ridge would float above the head — skipping it. I'm settling on layered eyes: a flattened dark-brown outer sphere, a smaller black sphere, and two tiny highlights for sparkle.

For whiskers, I'm placing four per side radiating from a muzzle point near the nose, calculating the dome's local half-width at that depth so the whisker roots sit flush against the curved muzzle surface.

I'm working out whisker endpoints spread in y to fan them naturally, using a thin dark rod material rather than pure black for a softer look, and considering whether to add subtle pink cheek blush as flattened spheres positioned just below the eyes on the dome surface.

Beyond that, I'm thinking about additional fur details like a darker dorsal countershading streak, small fur tufts at the cheeks and rump, and possibly a scent gland marking to add realism.

For the capybara, a signature nose bump makes sense as a dark ellipsoid near the snout top. Then I'm shifting to the bird companion's whimsical traits — blush cheeks, a tiny crest, a white belly, and toon-cel shaded blue body with a countershaded orange belly, giving it that classic bluebird charm.

Refining the bird body color zones...

Switching to flat colors for the feathers instead of cel-shading, then setting up the bird's joint hierarchy—body, head, and beak joints with their positions and parent relationships for the rig.

Now defining the lower beak with jaw role while treating the upper beak as fixed to the head, then setting up wing joints at the shoulder with hinge directions toward the tip and assigning them a "wing" role for rigging.

For the tail, I'm adding a joint at the base with a slight upward-backward direction and a "tail" role. For legs, I'm deciding between a simple single-joint leg role versus a small chain, leaning toward a minimal chain with rod geometry and orange toe capsules extending forward.

Realizing the legs are mostly tucked inside the body and barely visible, I'm raising the bird's overall center height slightly so a bit of leg shows below the belly fluff, then adjusting all dependent part positions relative to a new base-height constant.

Now I'm defining the bird's body, head, and tail using scaled sphere geometries at specific offsets from that base height, and starting to sketch out a beak using a spike/sweep helper that takes a base point, direction, length, radius, and color.

Adding eyes and feather texture cards...

I'm adding a second tuft paint variant, slightly darker/mottled, so the cards blend naturally with the body coat rather than looking noisy. I'll scatter extra cards on the head with tighter spacing and a filter to keep them away from the snout, and I'm considering whether legs need their own card scatter too.

Skipping the chest ruff for now. For eyes, I'll place sphere geometry parts on the head bone at specific offsets, and I'm double-checking that mixing tuple coordinates with bone attachments still works correctly. Ears get a dark brown outer rim with a pink inner color to match a capybara's hairless inner ear, and I'm leaving the mouth line simple for now rather than adding a full jaw outline.

I'm adding a thin dark vertical philtrum line running from the nose down to the lip, estimating the coordinates even though there's some risk the geometry ends up slightly inside or outside the head surface. I'm working through the dome math to figure out where the front face surface sits at a given height, approximating the curvature so the facial features line up with the head's rounded shape.

Now I'm placing teeth boxes near the mouth, checking their z-depth against the jaw surface curve to make sure they sit properly within the lower jaw sweep.

For the nose, I'm centering a dark pad with radii that extend slightly past the head's front apex, giving it a natural protrusion. I'm adding two small dark nostril ellipsoids on the pad's front surface, calculating their z-position so they sit flush against the curved pad surface, though I'm second-guessing whether nostrils should actually sit higher on top for a more whimsical capybara look.

Now I'm positioning the tail nub as a small sphere near the rump's end, working out coordinates based on the body path's starting point and the rump's downward shift, then placing hind legs symmetrically at the hips where I'm checking the body radius to make sure the legs sit just inside the body contour at that z-depth.

Adding thigh and shoulder bulges as painted ellipsoid parts attached at the hip and shoulder joints, using radii slightly larger than the leg root to give richer muscle shape, then moving on to the limb chain results.

Now I'm setting up the leg chains: naming joints per side (shoulder/elbow/wrist for front, hip/knee/ankle style for hind), assigning paint colors to the sweeps, and deciding role tags ("leg" vs "arm") for contact behavior. I'm confirming that passing a Vector3 path array into the chain builder works fine since it defaults to polyline knots with spans equal to points minus one, so no reach checking is needed before building the three-segment hind limb.

I'm verifying the hind limb geometry — checking root-to-target distance against total segment lengths to make sure the bend directions (knee forward, hock back) produce a plausible shape, and noting the toes should extend forward in the +Z direction from the foot. With the geometry confirmed, I'm moving to write the actual body sweep code using the radius-function and color options for each sweep call.

For the radius profile, I'll use the existing `interpolate` helper exported from the sweep module to smoothly blend a handful of keyframed width/depth values across the body's length, giving it a rounded, organic taper instead of linear creasing.

I'm noticing the head ends up taller than the back, making it look oddly whimsical, so I'm lowering the head stations slightly and adjusting the bird's position to compensate. I'll define the head center positions as a function of z so the nostril and other dependent features recompute automatically.

Rather than track that function symbolically, it's simpler to just shift everything down by 0.02 and recompute: eyes, blush, nose pad, nostrils, gland bump, teeth, philtrum, whisker base, jaw sweep, jaw joint, and ear positions all get the same offset applied.

I'm also checking the daisy center, bird head, and body-neck path joints to make sure the chain connects smoothly from the body end through the neck segments up to the head, verifying the z-values line up along the sweep.

Checking that the head joint parents correctly to the neck's second joint, and confirming the overall body proportions (head slightly forward and above body center) look visually reasonable before tallying up the total figure height.

I'm verifying the floor contact points: setting leg, paw pad, and toe capsule radii and y-offsets so all feet touch y=0 cleanly, then noting where paint/ink colors apply for the head and pupils.

Now I'm working out the jaw sweep geometry, making sure the path arrays and radius function are typed correctly as tuples for TypeScript.

For the ear, I'm figuring out rotation and scale ordering so it composes properly before rotating outward. Then for the daisy, I'm setting up a ring of petals using a frame-based arrangement, building each petal as an elongated sphere geometry scaled thin and positioned on stems attached to the head bone.

I'm checking that each petal's flattened axis aligns with the flower's normal direction so it lies flat in the flower plane, with the ring radius set small to form a tight daisy center.

Actually the total diameter was getting too large relative to the head, so I'm rescaling the petal dimensions and ring radius smaller — translating y by .011, shrinking the center sphere to radius .01 in yellow, and confirming the ring callback's type signature is compatible even though it returns a value. Then I move on to the fur cards using scattered hit points, and start thinking through the skin surface setup for the body.

Setting up imports...

Defining coat shader layers...

Building skeleton joints...

Now I'm setting up the body sweep and looping through both sides to build front limbs with IK targets, checking that segment lengths roughly match the hip-to-foot distances.

Adding shoulder sphere and paw placement details...

Still defining leg geometry...

Now moving to the head, lofting a series of stations along the skull from brow to nose with varying widths and heights to shape its profile.

I'm checking whether the head cap's end radius might overlap or poke through the body's surface near the neck, since the head sphere cap at z~.38 could extend beyond the body's shrinking radius there—needs adjusting so the head blends cleanly into the body rather than clipping through it.

Good, that offset works. Now I'm adding inner ear detail and whisker sizing, then moving to the bird: setting body joint position and head placement, with wing ellipsoids angled downward at the rear using an x-axis rotation to tilt the long axis.

Working out feather placement...

Checking the shape closes properly without self-crossing, then moving to feather coloring—settling on a simple flat blue "#1f5aa8" rather than white-tipped variants since bluebirds don't have that marking. Now I'm setting up the tail feathers with extruded coordinates and verifying the x and y axes are perpendicular by checking their dot product.

Still placing crest spikes, eyes with highlights, and beak geometry...

I'm finishing the beak with a lower bone-colored spike, then sketching legs and orange feet, and confirming body paint is defined before moving to minor details like fluff texture and an eyelash option. Now I'm generating the tuft texture as an SVG path shape.

I'm tinting the card feathers with a mottled tan-brown paint shaded by surface normal, then scattering head feathers onto the head loft region filtered by normal direction and z-position to keep them within the face area.

I need to exclude cards that would poke into the bird's body near its feet, so I'm filtering out hits within a box around the bird's lower body. Now I'm moving on to the eye rim and jaw coloring, then starting the whisker geometry with a nested loop building base points along the snout.

Still writing whisker rods...

Then I'll add a small tail nub sphere and consider whether to add a darker nose-bridge detail to the head coat for extra realism.

I'm second-guessing whether to add a smile curve near the philtrum, checking if sample points land on the dome surface at various heights, but decide it's getting too fiddly—better to skip the smile and rely on blush and teeth for the whimsical look instead.

Now I'm settling on a plan: just write the complete module in one go rather than yielding partway through, then give a brief summary after. I'm double-checking the type signatures for the helper functions (spike, capsule, part) to make sure the arguments like color fills, scale vectors, and rotation tuples all line up correctly before finalizing the code.

Writing bird joint hierarchy...
